author: DamiLee
description:
A real city survived 30 years of sieges, not with walls or armies, but because the ocean itself swallowed the only road in.

Mont Saint-Michel sits off the coast of Normandy on a tidal island where the sea becomes the defense. When the tide rolls in, the causeway vanishes. The island becomes unreachable. No fortress. No military garrison. Just a monastery perched on a rock, with an abbey at its crown instead of a keep.

And yet it held through nearly every English siege during the Hundred Years War.

The landscape did what armies couldn't.

If that sounds familiar, it should. The same logic is built into Minas Tirith, where every level of the city is both a spiritual ascent and a defensive layer, with the Citadel and the White Tower rising at the top. Tolkien wasn't just building fantasy architecture. He was drawing from something that already existed.

The real version is in France. It's been standing for centuries. And the tide still comes in.

title: Why England Couldn't Conquer This Island for 30 Years
